name: Kaska
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Moore, Patrick J. 2002. Point of View in Kaska Historical Narratives. PhD diss., Indiana University (includes Kaska grammar/phonology sketch); also Meek 2001 (U. Arizona PhD); neither reachable online

new_statements.quote: 11.—Un point très important de la phonétique nahanaise est l'hiatus que je rends par le point en haut (˙). Il a pour effet de faire hausser la voix sur la syllabe qui le précède et de couper, pour ainsi dire, le mot en deux [...]. 12.—Enfin le nahanais possède un accent très clairement défini marqué du signe ʹ qui fait appuyer considérablement sur la syllabe qui en est affectée. Cet accent très sensible dans certains mots, surtout ceux d'origine tlinket, est moins apparent chez d'autres sur la désinence desquels il se porte tout particulièrement.
new_statements.translation: 11.—A very important point of Nahanais phonetics is the hiatus [glottal catch], which I render by the raised dot (˙). Its effect is to raise the voice on the syllable preceding it and, so to speak, to cut the word in two [...]. 12.—Finally, Nahanais has a very clearly defined accent, marked with the sign ʹ, which makes one bear down considerably on the syllable affected by it. This accent, very perceptible in certain words, above all those of Tlingit origin, is less apparent in others, on whose ending [final syllable] it falls most particularly.
new_statements.citation: [Morice, Adrien-Gabriel]. [1899]. Précis de grammaire nahanaise: phonétique nahanaise. S.l.: s.n., 72 pp. (MPG PuRe item_403671; CIHM 18392).
new_statements.locator: Article premier (Phonétique nahanaise), 'Des sons', §12 (with §11), printed p. 5 = PDF p. 3 of the MPG scan
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK:, PDF p.3 = printed p.5, 'Des Sons' §§11-12, read from the page image (the scanned layer is garbled but the scan is clear). §11 and §12 are there word for word as quoted; the reader's [...] elides only the end of §11 ('en interrompant brusquement la prononciation de la syllabe qui peut le suivre') and its small-print note ('Préfixé à un mot... suffixé à une désinence, il fait élever le ton et occasionne un arrêt subit de la voix sur cette désinence'). Translation is fair. IDENTITY (fails): the Précis does not describe Kaska. I fetched sources Morice's published account, 'The Nah·ane and their language', Trans. Canadian Institute 7 (1902-3 [1904]): 517-534 (archive.org nahanethei…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Morice, native words carry a (weakly realized) accent on the word ending, i.e. the final syllable (which in Athabaskan nouns/verbs is the stem); in some words, especially Tlingit loanwords, the accent is much more salient and Morice marks its position lexically with ʹ. Modern descriptions instead treat Kaska as a tone language (marked high tone; long vowels also rising/falling) and give no stress-placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Words of Tlingit origin have a strongly audible accent (position marked word by word); §11: a glottal 'hiatus' raises the pitch of the preceding syllable (a tone/glottalization effect, not stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, impressionistic 1899 missionary description of 'nahanais'; final-syllable reading could equally be read as stem (morphological-root) prominence. Meek 2001:105 (Pelly Banks/Liard Kaska) presupposes stress ('[ɛ] and [ɪ] in unstressed positions'; 'vowel length may be phonemic, due to stress...') but never locates it and states 'Kaska is also a tonal language, having high, low, rising and falling tones'; Moore & Tuttle 2003 describe phonemic high tone, declination and phrase-final lengthening only.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes 'le nahanais' — Morice's Nah·ane, his cover term for the Tahltan–Kaska(–Tagish) 'Nahane' Dene; MPG PuRe (ISO kkz), CIHM and Glottolog all catalogue the work under Kaska, but the ms. itself names no consultants, locality or dialect. Internal cues point at least partly toward Tahltan (tahl1239) or a Stikine/Dease-area variety rather than Yukon Kaska: Morice says Nahanais has only one nasal vowel ('an'), whereas Kaska has a full nasal series, and gives 'lue' for 'fish' (Tahltan łuwe; Kaska łūge, cf. 'Łūge łēt'e' in the 1994 Ross River curriculum). A reviewer should resolve this (e.g. via Morice 1904) before filing the statement under kask1239. The modern Kaska sources read (Meek 2001: Pelly Banks with Liard/Stone data; Moore & Tuttle 2003; YNLC Yukon dialects) are unambiguously Kaska but give no stress-placement rule.

sources.note: Art. I §12 (printed p.5): 'le nahanais possède un accent très clairement défini' marked with ʹ, strongly pressing on the affected syllable; very noticeable in some words (esp. Tlingit loans), less apparent in others, where it falls particularly on the ending (désinence = final syllable). §11 separately describes the glottal 'hiatus' raising the voice on the preceding syllable.

sources.citation: Meek, Barbra Allyn. 2001. Kaska language socialization, acquisition and shift. PhD dissertation, University of Arizona (hdl:10150/290390).
sources.note: p.105 ('A Brief Kaska Grammar', Pelly Banks dialect with Liard data): inventory tables; 'Note: [ɛ] and [ɪ] in unstressed positions are not contrastive or predictable.' and 'Vowel length may be phonemic, due to stress, morphological merging, or a combination of these. Kaska is also a tonal language, having high, low, rising and falling tones.' Stress is presupposed but its position is never stated.

sources.note: Kaska 'has phonemic high tones'; short vowels H or L, long vowels L/H/rising/falling; acoustic study of 308 syllables finds F0 declination, no final lowering, significant phrase-final vowel lengthening. No statement about word stress.
